silu-048.title: Baragwanathia, a clubmoss ahead of its time
silu-048.text: Most plants of the Middle Silurian stood less than 10 cm tall. Baragwanathia had leaves that alone could match that height. This clubmoss, known from Australia, Canada and China, carried branching stems and needle-like leaves 10–20 cm long, and it looks advanced for its age. It belongs to the lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving lineages of vascular plants, which are plants with internal tubes for moving water. The lineage goes back to about 425 million years ago. One early lycophyte order, the Drepanophycales, lasted from the Late Silurian to the Late Devonian, roughly 430 to 360 million years ago.

silu-052.title: Kerrera's millipedes, among the first animals ashore
silu-052.text:
On the small Scottish island of Kerrera, rocks about 425 million years old hold the oldest definite millipedes. Two species, Kampecaris obanensis and Archidesmus, settle the question that older, vaguer fossils leave open. Millipedes are among the oldest known land animals, and among the first animals of any kind to colonize land.

Kerrera is not alone. Air-breathing arthropods from Ludlow, in England, date to about 420 million years ago. Both sites are older than the zircon age of Pneumodesmus, another early land walker met in {{ref:silu-061}}, whose own date is disputed. These small creatures were pioneers, but quiet ones. Land animals made little impact on Earth as a whole until they diversified in the Devonian, when soils, forests and food webs on land became far richer.

silu-049.title: Palaeoscolecid worms make their final appearance
silu-049.text: A lineage of worms that had crawled through the seafloor since the late Early Cambrian vanished in the Ludfordian. These were the palaeoscolecids, armored with tiny plates along their bodies. Their last fossils appear in this age, and {{ref:silu-054}} may have been what finished them off.

silu-051.title: Ice returns and the sea drains off the shelves
silu-051.text: The last major glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian. As ice grew on land in the middle of the age, it locked away seawater, and the oceans pulled back in a major regression, a retreat of the sea from the coasts. Vast new land lay exposed. Life moved in fast: plants and mats of cyanobacteria, the photosynthesizing microbes, quickly colonized the bare ground, pushing plant diversification further. The same cold snap is tied to {{ref:silu-054}}, the extinction that followed.

silu-054.title: The Lau event, the Silurian's last extinction
silu-054.text:
Conodonts, tiny eel-like animals with teeth, took the hardest blow in the last of three Silurian extinctions. It began at the start of the late Ludfordian and is named after Lau parish on the island of Gotland. Graptolites, colonial floating animals, suffered in the Kozlowskii event just after, which may have been the same crisis.

The timing points to a cause. The event coincided with a glacially driven global sea-level low, part of {{ref:silu-051}}, and most major groups saw higher extinction rates. Rated 6.2 in severity, it permanently altered marine communities. In the gap, stromatolites and microbial mats spread, the same pattern seen after the end-Ordovician and end-Permian extinctions. It may also have ended the palaeoscolecid worms.

silu-055.title: Sea scorpions at the height of their reign
silu-055.text: Acutiramus, a Late Silurian sea scorpion, reached about 2 m long. Sea scorpions, or eurypterids, were major parts of Silurian marine faunas, and most of their groups are first recorded in Silurian rocks. Their diversity peaked in the Pridoli, 423 to 419.2 million years ago. One group, the eurypterines, make up 90% of the eurypterids in most beds. Large pterygotids, with rudder-like tails and big pincers, also appeared in the Late Silurian. The most abundant of all was Eurypterus, which lived from about 432 million years ago to the end of the Pridoli. Pennsylvania's Tonoloway Formation holds a mass assemblage of them.

silu-056.title: The oldest sac fungi
silu-056.text: Most familiar molds and yeasts belong to the ascomycetes, or sac fungi. The earliest known members date from 423 to 419 million years ago, in the Silurian. They belong to a larger group, the dikaryan fungi, which began expanding and diversifying during this period.

silu-059.title: Charcoal marks the first wildfires
silu-059.text: Fire needs fuel and it needs oxygen. By the Pridoli, both were finally present. The first charcoal in the fossil record appears in this epoch, showing that atmospheric oxygen had risen high enough to sustain wildfires. Silurian charcoal suggests oxygen had crossed about 15% of the air, the threshold for burning. From here on, fire becomes a recurring force in the history of land plants.

silu-062.title: The Šilalė event strikes the conodonts
silu-062.text: Early in the Pridoli, conodonts suffered another extinction, the Šilalė event. It is marked by a negative carbon isotope excursion, a sudden shift in the chemistry of carbon, traced from cores in Lithuania to the Appalachian Basin of North America. While conodonts declined, brachiopods grew in diversity and abundance. The crisis coincided with the Pridoli's weakest 405,000-year cycle in the shape of Earth's orbit.

silu-061.title: Pneumodesmus, the oldest known air breather
silu-061.text:
Small holes in a fossil's skin made it famous. Pneumodesmus newmani, a millipede-like myriapod from Scotland, has openings in its cuticle read as spiracles, the breathing pores of a tracheal system. That makes it the earliest known arthropod built to breathe air, and among the oldest creatures known to have lived on land.

Its age, though, is disputed. It was once put at about 428 million years old, in the Wenlock. A 2023 study defended the Wenlock age, about 430 million years ago. Zircon dates and a 2025 study instead favor the Pridoli to Lochkovian, about 414 million years ago. Either way, it belongs with the millipedes, which first appear in the Silurian as among the oldest known land animals.

silu-063.title: Arachnids and centipedes join the millipedes
silu-063.text: Millipedes did not have the land to themselves for long. By the Pridoli, about 420 million years ago, centipedes and trigonotarbid arachnids, extinct spider relatives, had joined them. Timelines list the earliest trigonotarbids and land scorpions at about the same date. Some of the newcomers were predators, so there must have been prey, which ate plants or detritus, the dead remains of living things. Simple food webs had formed on land. Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods all became fully terrestrial during the Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution.

silu-064.title: Andreolepis, perhaps the first ray-finned fish
silu-064.text: Almost every fish alive today, from tuna to goldfish, is a ray-finned fish, with fins held up by thin bony rods. The earliest known member of the group may be Andreolepis hedei, about 420 million years old, found in Russia, Sweden and Estonia. Timelines put the first ray-finned fish at about the same date. The group took a long time to hit its stride. Its crown group, the lineage that includes all living members, arose much later, near the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary.

silu-065.title: The Iapetus closes and Laurussia is born
silu-065.text: An entire ocean disappeared by the end of the Silurian. The Iapetus Ocean had closed completely by about 420 million years ago, leaving a seam called the Iapetus Suture. Avalonia and Baltica fused with Laurentia in the Caledonian orogeny, a mountain-building collision, and formed Laurussia. That continent would later become the northern part of Pangaea. Convergence between Laurentia and Avalonia, and subduction of the Iapetus seafloor, had ceased by about 420 million years ago. The collision shaped Laurussia's southern margin, and rocks in Scandinavia's thrust sheets reached peak metamorphism, their deepest heating and squeezing, at about the same time.

silu-066.title: Ascocerid nautiloids vanish
silu-066.text: The ascocerids, an odd group of shelled cephalopods, came back from near-ruin once. Cut back by the end-Ordovician extinction, they recovered in the Silurian. Then, at the end of the Silurian, they died out abruptly.

silu-067.title: Seas fall and salt fills the Salina basin
silu-067.text: Sea level had risen through the first half of the Silurian and fell through the rest. At the period's end it dropped again, leaving evaporite basins, where seawater dried into salt, from Michigan to West Virginia. A warm, arid climate over a shallow inland basin laid down the Salina Group evaporites, 120–800 m thick. Meanwhile the new mountains eroded rapidly.

devo-001.title: Jawed fishes take over in the Age of Fishes
devo-001.text:
The Devonian earned its popular name, the Age of Fishes, honestly. Jawed vertebrates had appeared in the late Ordovician, but only now did they become common. Fish variety rose greatly, especially among ostracoderms, placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks.

The family tree had already branched. By about 419 million years ago jawed fishes had split into three lines: placoderms, the armored fishes; bony fishes; and a clade of spiny sharks and early cartilaginous fish. Both cartilaginous and bony fishes diversified through the period and played a large role in Devonian seas. Among the bony fishes, the lobe-finned forms, such as coelacanths and lungfish, were the most diverse. That detail matters, because the lobe-fins are the group from which four-limbed animals would later come.

devo-003.title: The Chaitenia arc docks with Patagonia
devo-003.text: A chain of volcanic islands called Chaitenia crashed into Patagonia during the Devonian. Its remains sit in what is now south-central Chile. The event was part of a larger change: Patagonia's margin turned convergent, with crust moving together, which led to a collision that began in the mid-Carboniferous.

devo-006.title: Kola's alkaline volcanoes
devo-006.text: Russia's Kola Peninsula holds an estimated 15,000 ± 2,700 cubic km of Devonian igneous rock. Magmas there built carbonatites, kimberlite pipes and the large nepheline syenite massifs of Khibiny and Lovozero. They came from small melt fractions of garnet peridotite beneath lithosphere about 200 km thick. This Kola large igneous province erupted about when the Viluy and Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets provinces did, and is a suggested trigger of the {{ref:devo-084}}.

devo-007.title: Roots pull carbon dioxide from the sky
devo-007.text: Plants changed the air simply by putting down roots. As land plants spread through the Devonian, carbon dioxide levels dropped steeply. Roots broke up rock and increased silicate weathering, a chemical reaction that locks carbon dioxide away; carbonates formed in ancient soils record it. The growing plant cover probably also buffered carbon dioxide while anoxic events in the oceans grew longer. The long-term fall in carbon dioxide, together with rising oxygen, led on to the late Paleozoic icehouse.

devo-009.title: Oxygen climbs toward modern levels
devo-009.text: Early in the Silurian, the air held only about 13% of today's oxygen level. By the end of the Devonian it was near modern. Early in the Devonian oxygen was still fairly low, possibly about half of modern values. The climb from 470 to 400 million years ago, called the Paleozoic Oxidation Event, is explained by early plants trapping organic carbon in sediments, so that it could not use up oxygen by decaying. As plants spread over the continents, they buried more carbon still. The richer air may have favored vertebrates able to breathe it, helping push tetrapods onto land.

devo-011.title: Placoderms, the armored rulers of Devonian waters
devo-011.text: Placoderms burst onto the scene at the very start of the Devonian, already in seemingly sudden diversity. These armored jawed fishes went on to dominate almost every known aquatic ecosystem, fresh water and salt water alike. One group, the petalichthyids, peaked early in the period and lived worldwide. A 419-million-year-old placoderm, Entelognathus, had a bony mouth skeleton like a bony fish's, a hint of how the groups are related. At the top end, giants such as Dunkleosteus grew up to seven meters long.

devo-002.title: The Caledonian mountains begin to collapse
devo-002.text: Mountains can fall under their own weight. After Baltica's margin was subducted and overridden by nappes, huge sheets of rock, the Caledonian mountain belt began to collapse in the Early Devonian. Burial peaked about 410 million years ago, recorded in Norway's Western Gneiss Region, and those rocks were brought back up about 400–385 million years ago. The collapse stretched and lowered the crust, and in Scandinavia it lasted a long time.

devo-005.title: Jawless armored fishes peak, then fade
devo-005.text: Cephalaspis, the most advanced jawless fish, appeared about 415 million years ago. Its kind, the armored jawless ostracoderms, peaked in diversity in the Early Devonian, and so did the scale-covered thelodonts. Both then declined. By the Middle Devonian jawed fishes were thriving while the ostracoderms dwindled, never to recover.

devo-008.title: The last of the radiodonts
devo-008.text: The radiodonts, the group of Cambrian predators that includes Anomalocaris, outlasted the Cambrian by a very long way. Their last appearance comes in the Early Devonian. One late survivor was Schinderhannes bartelsi, from Germany.

devo-010.title: Asian blocks drift away and open the Paleo-Tethys
devo-010.text: Pieces of future Asia were once part of Gondwana. North and South China, along with Tarim, rifted from Gondwana's northern margin, and a new ocean, the Paleo-Tethys, opened behind them. South China and Indochina had split away in the Silurian and moved north, shrinking the older Proto-Tethys ahead of them. South China and Annamia, today's Southeast Asia, later collided in the Carboniferous. The blocks did not go far at first. Their Devonian fossils resemble Australian species more than north Asian ones.

devo-012.title: The Rheic Ocean begins to close
devo-012.text: At the start of the Devonian, a wide ocean, the Rheic, separated Laurussia from Gondwana. In the Early Devonian it began to shrink. Gondwana moved toward Euramerica as the Rheic seafloor was subducted, pulled down beneath the plates. Near the end of the Early Devonian, two small blocks, Franconia and Saxothuringia, struck Laurussia and pinched out the eastern part of the ocean. The closure would not finish until the Mississippian, when Gondwana and Laurentia collided to form Pangaea.

devo-013.title: The Old Red Sandstone builds a red continent
devo-013.text: So many red rocks formed in this age that a whole continent took their name. Old Red Sandstone sediments began accumulating around 419 million years ago across Britain, Ireland, Norway, northeastern North America, Greenland and Svalbard. These mostly Devonian rocks were laid down in varied settings from the late Silurian into the earliest Carboniferous. Their red beds gave Laurussia the nickname Old Red Sandstone Continent. In Scotland, uplifted Silurian rocks eroded into fresh water, probably large river deltas, between 408 and 370 million years ago. Around 370 million years ago, at Siccar Point, rainy-season rivers near the equator laid iron-rich sands that winds then reworked into dunes.

devo-014.title: Lobe-finned fishes appear and divide
devo-014.text: The first lobe-finned fishes, about 418 million years ago, looked a lot like spiny sharks. Little hinted at what they would become. In the Early Devonian, between 416 and 397 million years ago, they split into two main lineages: the coelacanths and the rhipidistians. While placoderms dominated the seas, some lobe-fins moved into fresh water, between 416 and 385 million years ago. The coelacanths had their heyday later, in the Late Devonian and Carboniferous, from 385 to 299 million years ago.

devo-015.title: Arthropods settle coasts and floodplains
devo-015.text: By about 415 million years ago, numerous arthropods lived along coasts and on alluvial plains, the flat land beside rivers, and some were eating plants. Early rooted plants had built the first stable soils. Mites, scorpions, trigonotarbids and myriapods made homes in them. Land animals began to have a major impact on Earth only once they diversified in the Devonian.

devo-020.title: The first true nautilids
devo-020.text: The order of the living chambered nautilus has roots around 410 million years ago. Rutocerina, the earliest true nautilid, had a shell like those of the oncocerid nautiloids, its likely ancestors. Nautilids then flourished as their cousins declined: by the Middle Devonian there were about 22 genera, while other nautiloids dwindled.

devo-022.title: Rhynie chert, an ecosystem frozen in stone
devo-022.text: Hot springs in Scotland turned a whole community to stone. Silica-rich water from volcanic springs petrified plants, fungi, lichens and animals in place, almost instantly. The result is the Rhynie chert, formed about 410 million years ago in the Pragian. It is one of the first known fully terrestrial ecosystems, caught at an early stage of land colonization. Its animals include euthycarcinoids, branchiopods, arachnids and hexapods, and Rhyniognatha, possibly the oldest insect, is known from its jaws. The plants were rootless and leafless, and fungi living among them suggest fungi played a large role in plants' move onto land. The chert also holds the last nematophytes, enigmatic land organisms known since the Silurian.

devo-023.title: Trimerophytes and the start of the leafy plants
devo-023.text: Ferns, seed plants and most of the green world belong to one great clade, the euphyllophytes. Its early members are known from Early Devonian fossils. Among them were the trimerophytes, a class of early vascular plants known only from the Devonian. Timeline of life puts the earliest trimerophytes and lycophytes at 410 million years ago.

devo-019.title: Ammonoids coil into existence
devo-019.text: Ammonoids, with their tightly coiled shells, began as straight shells. The earliest appeared in the Emsian, around 410–408 million years ago, descended from straight-shelled bactritid nautiloids. Transitional fossils show the shell coiling step by step. Bactritids also first appear in the Early Devonian, and their radiation alongside the ammonoids may reflect falling oxygen in deeper water. One early group, the agoniatitids, radiated in the Emsian, and a new order, the Goniatitida, arose before 391.9 million years ago and gave rise to later ammonoid orders. The line would become abundant in the Mesozoic and vanish around the end-Cretaceous extinction.

devo-024.title: Tungsenia and the fish ancestors of tetrapods
devo-024.text: Every four-limbed animal traces its roots to a group of Devonian fishes, the tetrapodomorphs. The oldest known member, Tungsenia from China, dates to about 409 million years ago. A little later, about 395 million years ago, a small Chinese lobe-fin called Kenichthys shows the internal nostril, or choana, caught midway through its evolution. This group did well for itself. Its relatives became the most numerous bony fishes of Devonian and Carboniferous rivers and streams.

devo-025.title: Jaekelopterus, the largest arthropod ever
devo-025.text: A single claw from Germany's Klerf Formation reveals the largest arthropod ever known. It belonged to the sea scorpion Jaekelopterus rhenaniae. Complete, this pincer would have been about 45.5 cm long. Size did not save the group. Eurypterines lost over half their diversity within 10 million years in the Early Devonian.

devo-026.title: Pyrite-coated fossils of the Hunsrück Slate
devo-026.text: Many fossils in Germany's Hunsrück Slate wear a coat of pyrite, the shiny iron mineral. Dating from the latest Pragian to early Emsian, it is one of few marine Devonian Lagerstätten, sites that preserve soft tissue. Its fauna includes the trilobite Chotecops and the puzzling placoderm Stensioella.

devo-028.title: Rhyniognatha and the first insects
devo-028.text: The oldest proposed insect is known only from a pair of jaws. Rhyniognatha hirsti is about 400 million years old, but whether it really is an insect is contested. The first possible insect fossils appear around 416 million years ago. Early Devonian rocks of about 400 million years ago preserve only a few kinds of insects, and none could fly. The group that would later outnumber all other animals began small and grounded.

devo-031.title: Laurussia completed
devo-031.text: By about 400 million years ago, Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and smaller terranes had collided in the Caledonian orogeny to form Laurussia, also called Euramerica. In Scotland's northwest Highlands, part of the Iapetus Ocean closed as Laurentia met Baltica. The collision raised a string of mountain ranges along the new continent's southeastern coast. Laurussia lay in the dry belt along the Tropic of Capricorn, then drifted north and turned counterclockwise. Low seas in the Early Devonian split its seafloor animals into separate provinces, which were united again by the Middle Devonian.

devo-032.title: Lungfish and the dipnoan renaissance
devo-032.text: Lungfish appeared about 400 million years ago and evolved so quickly that the burst is called the dipnoan renaissance. By the Middle Devonian, 397–385 million years ago, they had evolved proto-lungs and proto-limbs. These let them spend spells outside the water.

devo-033.title: Sharks and their kin arrive
devo-033.text: Shark-like scales go back to the Ordovician, but the oldest unambiguous fossils of cartilaginous fishes are Middle Devonian. By about 395 million years ago these fishes, the sharks, rays and chimaeras, had appeared, evolving from acanthodians, the spiny sharks. Their skeletons are made of cartilage rather than bone. They quickly became diverse and important in Devonian seas.

openers.ludlow-epoch: In the Ludlow, the land was still nearly empty, but the first settlers had arrived. Clubmoss-like lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving plant lineages, date to about 425 million years ago, and so do the oldest definite millipedes, from Kerrera in Scotland. At sea, the story turned harsher. A final glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian and is tied to the Lau event, the last of three Silurian extinctions, which may have ended the ancient palaeoscolecid worms. Sea scorpions and the earliest sac fungi were close behind.
openers.pridoli-epoch: The Pridoli, the last and shortest epoch of the Silurian, saw the land come alive. Oxygen rose high enough for the first wildfires, and Scotland's Pneumodesmus is among the oldest creatures known to have breathed air on land. By about 420 million years ago, millipedes shared the ground with centipedes and spider relatives, and the first ray-finned fish may have swum in the seas. Meanwhile the Iapetus Ocean closed entirely, and falling seas left salt basins from Michigan to West Virginia.
openers.devonian-period: The Devonian is popularly called the Age of Fishes, and with reason: jawed vertebrates, rare before, became common, and armored placoderms appeared in sudden diversity at its start. On land, the period's story is about plants. As they spread, carbon dioxide dropped steeply, and oxygen, only a fraction of today's level in the early Silurian, rose to near-modern levels. Beneath it all, the crust kept moving, from an island arc docking with Patagonia to huge alkaline magmas on Russia's Kola Peninsula.
openers.early-devonian-epoch: The Early Devonian rearranged both the map and the tree of life. The Caledonian mountains began to collapse, the Rheic Ocean began to close, and Asian blocks pulled away from Gondwana to open the Paleo-Tethys. Red sediments spread over a continent that would be called the Old Red Sandstone Continent. In the water, lobe-finned fishes and the first ammonoids appeared while jawless armored fishes peaked and began to fade. On land, Scotland's Rhynie chert froze an early ecosystem of plants, fungi and arthropods in stone.

reviews.ludlow-epoch: The Ludlow shows life pushing onto land while the sea endured a crisis. Baragwanathia and the first millipedes were early pioneers ashore. In the Ludfordian, growing ice drained the seas from the shelves, exposing land that plants and microbial mats quickly colonized. The same sea-level low accompanied the Lau event, which hit conodonts hardest and may have ended the palaeoscolecid worms. Sea scorpions rode out the trouble and went on to peak in the Pridoli, as the first sac fungi appeared.
reviews.pridoli-epoch: In the Pridoli, life on land reached a new threshold. Oxygen crossed the level needed for fire, and air-breathing arthropods such as Pneumodesmus, then centipedes and arachnids, built the first simple food webs ashore. In the sea, the Šilalė event cut the conodonts back, ascocerid nautiloids vanished, and the first ray-finned fish appeared. All the while, the Iapetus Ocean closed into Laurussia, and falling seas left thick salt deposits as the new mountains wore away.
reviews.devonian-period: The Devonian's big themes connect. Plants spreading over the land drew down carbon dioxide and buried organic carbon, letting oxygen climb toward modern levels. That richer air may have favored vertebrates that could breathe it. Meanwhile, the seas filled with jawed fishes, led by the armored placoderms, and the crust stayed busy, with the Chaitenia arc docking in Patagonia and Kola's magmas erupting at about the time of a later extinction.
reviews.early-devonian-epoch: The Early Devonian was a time of separation and assembly. Laurussia was completed while the Caledonian mountains collapsed, the Rheic Ocean began to close and the Paleo-Tethys opened behind departing Asian blocks. In the water, jawed fishes rose as jawless ones faded: lobe-fins split into coelacanths and rhipidistians, tetrapodomorphs and lungfish appeared, and cartilaginous fishes followed. On land, rooted plants made the first stable soils, and fossil sites such as the Rhynie chert record arthropods, fungi, and perhaps the first insect living among them.
